headline: High: shared filesystem and broad tool/network access create default risks of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors between Goose and LightAgent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Goose can read/write the user filesystem and use MCP; its concurrency model shares state via filesystem. LightAgent also uses MCP and can observe/replace/block lifecycle payloads, so a shared file or MCP bridge can carry attacker-controlled instructions. The interaction is plausible in default setups, though not directly documented as a specific bridge.
conditions: IF Goose and LightAgent exchange files through the shared cwd, injected instructions can propagate.
IF LightAgent runtime hooks rewrite payloads before Goose consumes them, prompt content can be altered.
mitigations: Separate working directories for each agent.
Disable shared MCP servers unless provenance is enforced.
Add a manual review step before either agent consumes the other's files.
Log and diff all MCP payloads before execution.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to inter-agent messages.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Goose touches source code and files in cwd, while LightAgent handles conversations, memory, trace data, tool results, and workflow state. Both have broad network egress and can use MCP, so a shared workspace or copied artifacts can leak sensitive content from one agent into the other or onward. The pairwise leakage path is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same cwd, Goose can expose files that LightAgent later ingests.
IF LightAgent forwards tool results or memory to remote APIs, copied Goose artifacts can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces and separate credentials.
Redact secrets before passing artifacts between agents.
Turn off network egress for one agent during sensitive tasks.
Restrict shared files to a minimal allowlist.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Goose has unrestricted filesystem write, shell, git-state modification, and broad network egress; LightAgent has subprocess and browser execution plus MCP. If both run in the same directory or shared mutable resource, concurrent writes and git changes can race and corrupt state. The profiles explicitly show shared-state-via-filesystem for Goose and multiple-instance support for both.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or cwd, file and git races can occur.
IF either agent edits the same mutable resource without locking, last-writer-wins corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Serialize git writes with a lock file.
Disable concurrent runs on the same workspace.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
requires-engineering: add transactional workspace coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Goose can produce code, shell actions, and MCP-driven outputs; LightAgent consumes tool calls, tool results, provenance metadata, and workflow state. That makes it plausible for LightAgent to treat Goose output as authoritative and propagate mistakes into downstream actions. The profiles do not prove a mandatory trust chain, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF LightAgent uses Goose-generated files or messages as inputs without verification, errors can cascade.
IF Goose emits incorrect code or commands and LightAgent executes them, downstream harm can occur.
mitigations: Require human approval before execution of Goose outputs.
Add schema validation on inter-agent messages.
Compare outputs against independent checksums or tests.
Limit LightAgent to read-only review of Goose artifacts.
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware trust scoring.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and the available fields do not show a residency, certification, or retention mismatch. Goose handles model-provider keys and extension tokens; LightAgent handles API keys and TOT API keys, so compliance risk exists mainly if the operator routes regulated data through either agent. The pair itself does not evidence a specific mismatch, so low is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through either agent, retention and residency controls must be checked.
IF the operator stores secrets in shared files, compliance obligations may be triggered.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared workspaces.
Review retention settings before processing sensitive inputs.
Store secrets in a dedicated vault.
Document data flows for both agents.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention.
